utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis with Joanna Korner and our Case Manager Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We have been alerted that the Office of the Prosecution has a number of matters to raise before the witness is brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. I'm here to deal with the administrative matters this morning. Your Honours, the first of them is this. We received, I believe, last week, a Scheduling Order that said that the case of Rasic would be listed for the whole of January effectively and therefore because again of the problem with Your Honours being on a number of different cases, we would not be sitting for the whole of January. We respectfully suggest that it would be more logical and more sensible if we were to conclude the evidence in this case which we believe, and I've spoken certainly to Mr. Krgovic this morning, would be concluded in January. Indeed, I understand from Mr. Krgovic that he believes that his evidence will be concluded in December, at the beginning of December, which would enable us to call, if allowed, the rebuttal evidence that we have suggested in respect of the Stanisic case which is very limited, as Your Honours will have seen, or fairly limited at the moment. We're still doing one other investigation. So that the -- if we finish the evidence, there would then in any event be a gap whilst we deal with final briefs, and we would be hoping that Your Honours, and I believe this would be a joint application, would be allowing us six weeks between the conclusion of evidence and the filing of the briefs to deal with the Rasic case. So, Your Honour, I raise that. I raised it with -- by e-mail with both counsel for the Defence, and I'm not sure what their view is about this. The response I had from counsel for Stanisic was it depended really on how much rebuttal evidence we wanted to call. But, Your Honour, that's the first submission that we make, that we should conclude all the evidence and obviously any witnesses Your Honours want to call or decide to call in January, rather than the case being adjourned for the whole month. I don't know if Your Honours want to hear from either of the Defence before I move onto the next matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does either Defence counsel have a view on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I believe it does depend on whether -- and whether the -- how much rebuttal evidence will be -- the Office of the Prosecutor seek to introduce, and what would be -- would that be -- would they receive the leave from the Trial Chamber to do so. That's one question. The second question is, if the -- if the Trial Chamber intends to call any witnesses. If that is the case, then I think it makes a lot of sense that we are adjourned over the -- over January so we can -- we can prepare for that and for these witnesses and for the rebuttal witnesses and then continue in February. That is my opinion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what Mr. Zecevic has just said is basically the position of our Defence as well. Depending on how many witnesses will be called on rebuttal, and, of course, we still have to complete our case and then the Prosecution will reconsider if they need any rebuttal witnesses in respect of our Defence. I do agree that, as Mr. Zecevic said, if there are rebuttal witnesses and Court witnesses called, we should best adhere to the schedule which has already been adopted and continue with our presentation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of -- I accept there are a number of imponderables. May I say the reason I'm raising it is, one, because of the logicality of going on with our case, but secondly, because it does the affect the professional futures of some of the members of the Prosecution team. There are other cases on which they are due to work and the longer this one is stretched out, the more difficult it becomes for them. Your Honour, that is not me but for other members of the team. Your Honours, I raised it. I appreciate it is not something that can be decided now but so that the Your Honours can have a look at the pros and cons of carrying on with this case rather than interposing Rasic, not to mention whatever may happen in Haradinaj as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, counsel would appreciate, of course, that the -- the decision resulting in the Scheduling Order that was published would not have been taken casually and the difficulty in terms of scheduling Rasic has been patent since July. But the -- we -- we have the views which have been articulated this morning, and the -- Senior Legal Officers in the respective cases would, I suppose, be invited to look at it and the Judges involved may have a second look at it and return to -- and further consider this matter. And more than that I couldn't say at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That's the first administrative matter. Your Honours, the next, can I come to, relates to the Zupljanin witnesses and their alleged refusal to speak to the Office of the Prosecutor. Your Honour, on the 6th of July of this year, the -- His Honour Judge Harhoff asked about the question of witnesses being -- the Zupljanin witnesses speaking to the Prosecution. We had made a request to speak to all of them, including the 92 bis. And Mr. Krgovic announced that: "... Your Honour, there is no change in this position." It says "nor," I think it says "nor our witness" but that I believe must be not one witness is willing to meet with the Prosecution. And Judge Harhoff asked -- Mr. Hannis was dealing with it, and asked if that was right, and Judge Harhoff said: "My understanding from Mr. Krgovic's answer was that none of the witnesses to be called by Zupljanin are willing -- is that correct Mr. Krgovic?" "You are correct," said Mr. Krgovic. Your Honours, it is quite plain from the last two witnesses, we would submit, that the witnesses were not asked. I'm not saying that Mr. Krgovic was deliberately misleading the Court. I am, however, suggesting that if he isn't, he must have been misled by his investigators. Your Honours it was our intention not to interview the witnesses just before they gave evidence. Your Honours will recall that we'd strongly disapproved of this happening when the Defence saw the witnesses called for the Prosecution because we felt that it was undue pressure and, indeed, effectively what the Defence were doing was just proofing what were really their witnesses but being called by us. We wanted to interview, and still do, witnesses away from the court, those that are left. Your Honours, we've seen their response that was given to Mr. Hannis about the coming of the -- the witness who is coming today. However, we would now like Your Honours to order that we receive not later than seven days from today in writing from the witnesses, not from an investigator, the fact that they have been asked whether they're prepared to speak to the Prosecution and have declined to do so. Your Honours, we think in light of what has happened, that is only fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I call on Mr. Krgovic for a response, may I ask whether there is precedent for this course that you propose?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, that -- they be -- that an order be made like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the witnesses themselves to -- for the Court to order that the witnesses produce this -- the witnesses themselves state this in writing and file it with the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I honestly don't know. I have to say I don't recall this happening before, where we have been informed that witnesses will not or do not want to speak to us and it turns out that's not right. I'm not aware of that happening before, or if anybody is. But Your Honours have power to make whatever orders you think proper in the circumstances. And we would suggest in the circumstances of what has happened here, that's a proper order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Why I asked about precedent, apart from the -- what Judges -- what -- particularly in the common law is always criticised for being reluctant to do anything for the first time, is that it struck me as being a bit heavy-handed and I just wondered whether -- but that's the first impression. Let me hear from Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the alternative, and we didn't do that, of course, is we could have rung up each of the witnesses ourselves and asked them. And we decided not to do so because we didn't want any accusations that in some way we were attempting to interfere with the witnesses. In hindsight, we should have probably done that because we're perfectly entitled to that. There is no property in a witness. And if Your Honours prefer, we personally will ask for the all the contact details and ourselves speak to the witnesses. And, Your Honour, I'm very helpfully told by Mr. Hannis there is in fact a -- a decision on this point which is the Mrksic case, 1st of September, 2006, decision re the Prosecution motion to interview Defence witnesses. Whether it is right on point, I don't know. And I see Mr. Hannis is -- but there's some authority that has dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, quite apart from what Ms. Korner just said, when I said that I had a good idea of how I should overcome the problem, I gave an order to my investigators to take statements from the coming witnesses on this issue and to get back to me as soon as possible, and I did tell Ms. Korner that I would be giving her the responses from witnesses as soon as I have them. To dispel any suspicions or uncertainties, I've given such an order to my investigators irrespective of any orders that the Trial Chamber may issue. Your Honours, this isn't the first time that a misunderstanding arises surrounding the availability of witnesses. We did not complain with the Prosecution where we received information about Prosecution witnesses not being willing to talk to us, whereas, once they appeared here as witnesses, they would say that they thought that they weren't entitled to meet with the Defence. It happened on a number of occasions and, of course, it may be just down to simply the misunderstanding of witnesses not understanding the difference between just speaking and interviewing a witness. I did speak to one of these witnesses after their testimony, and this is precisely what emerged to be the problem. I will, as Ms. Korner suggested, I will take written statements from witnesses on these issues and get back to Ms. Korner on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, our complaint is that according to the witness on Friday he was never actually asked. That's the -- whether -- I accept entirely that some of the witnesses that the Defence asked to see originally said no, they wouldn't, but it turned out that was because they believed they weren't supposed to speak to the Defence. Your Honours, what our complaint is and why we are making this application is because it appears that, in fact, the first two witnesses had neither actually been asked by the investigators. So that's the reason. But if Mr. Krgovic says they're all being asked to make statements now that's -- but we would ask that we get it well in advance because if any of them are willing to talk to us who are coming at a later stage, then we would want to interview them well in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, did we put a deadline to that on a Wednesday, that Mr. Krgovic would inform us by -- wasn't it Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We gave Mr. Krgovic a delay to let us know by Wednesday. So -- and now I understand --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... in respect of the next the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, the next [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The next witness for -- to give us the answer for Friday end of business and the other ones for Wednesday. And now I understand, unless I'm wrong, that what you're asking for and what Mr. Krgovic is offering, if I may say, is basically the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Your Honours, the difference was that it was just for Mr. Krgovic to inform. I'm asking for written confirmation. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Wasn't that what you were offering, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will let the Trial Chamber know by Wednesday if any of the witnesses are willing to speak with the Prosecution. But irrespective of that, I will take statements on this issue from the coming witnesses and these will need to be translated and, of course, it will take some time. But I will, of course, meet the deadline set by which I will let the Trial Chamber know if any of the witnesses are willing to speak with the Prosecution and under what terms. At any rate, irrespective of the Chamber's decision, I wish to take written statements from witnesses which will then have to be translated to back up what I will say on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So by Wednesday, we will know. And written statements of the witnesses will follow. And -- and the -- the delay -- or the deadline proposed by the Prosecution seven weeks [sic] before the witness appears in court for the statements, would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness who is due to appear after the next one, who is already here, will give us the statement by Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it said seven weeks. I'm not sure that's -- I said seven days from today but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course, seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, all we're concerned about is that, particularly of some of the major witnesses, we don't want to be told we have to see them here because we're not prepared to do that at all. We -- as I said, we consider that an oppressive and unhelpful way of proceeding. Your Honours, can I move then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we leave this, may I only add this. Having regard to what have you said this morning, Ms. Korner, about the apparent misunderstanding of what was certainly canvassed on Friday, the -- may I suggest to Mr. Krgovic that in the instructions that he gives to his investigators, the -- what is being asked of the witnesses is clearly phrased so that there isn't this apparent misunderstanding, which, according to what you told us on Friday, has occurred in the past. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the third matter relates to our response to the Defence's application to change the mode of testimony of Witness SZ-012. Your Honours issued an oral ruling on Friday, which appeared to criticise the Prosecution for not putting in the transcript. But, Your Honours, I think there's some misunderstanding about this. Our response to the Defence's application to change the mode of testimony was we don't object, provided the whole of the transcript and the associated exhibits go in. And I'm assuming the Defence, in order to change the mode of testimony, must have put in the transcript. So I'm not clear how we should be criticised for not putting it in, if I may say so. So -- Your Honours, there is -- it's not our application. It's the Defence's, and we're simply saying if you want it in, we agree only on the basis of all it goes in. And I'm assuming and I believe that's right that Mr. Krgovic did attach the whole of the Brdjanin transcript. Where if he didn't that's his fault not ours. He's the one making the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, criticism was not in the mind of the Chamber when it issued the oral ruling. It was seeking the assistance, really, of the Prosecution in that the -- Mr. Krgovic, having indicated which portions of the transcript -- on which portions of the transcript he was relying, we -- were inviting the Prosecution to be more helpful in terms of identifying the portions of which they were relying. And this is not the first time that this has happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, sorry. We're saying the whole thing. And my understanding is how could -- he couldn't have possibly have put in a partial transcript. Well, Your Honours, in that case that's the Defence's fault. There it is. Because it is their application, they should put -- if we say this is it, they are to respond if they agree or not. And if they agree, then they can put in the whole transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if I'm not totally wrong, the Prosecution did exactly the same with a Prosecution witness, I think it was Todorovic but I'm not totally sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was -- yes, Your Honours. There was a -- there was a difference there in that there wasn't a question -- that was a dead witness. I mean, so -- and it was days and days of transcript. This is one day. But Your Honours, it's not our application -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We quite happy for this witness to stagger off to Sarajevo and be properly examined and cross-examined. We're trying to help. If the Defence agree, then -- to this then they can put in the whole transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree. However, in my view, the problem has arisen with the other part of the order. We are in agreement with the entire transcript being admitted into evidence. The problem lies with documents. When the Prosecution sought these documents, we don't have access to these documents from that case at all, and we are not clear on which other specific documents the Prosecution are interested in. Only once we know that can we give our position, and we think part of the transcript was confidential. The portion we received from the Prosecution was the one that we sought admission for. I don't know if there was some other part which not disclosed to us because perhaps it took place in a closed session. That was my understanding of the Trial Chamber's decision. Namely, that the Prosecution should deliver the entire transcript, save perhaps for parts that are not accessible, and the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't believe that's right. I don't believe part of it is in closed session. In any event, Your Honours, we're perfectly happy to provide the documents and, if necessary, the whole transcript. We will do that. My objection was to the way it was phrased which seems to suggest that we were in some way at fault. It's not the first time it's happened and I do take exception to that. But we will -- to make things easier we will deliver up the whole transcript plus the associated exhibits. And I don't think it's right that any of it was in closed session and confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the matter has been revolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honours, can I move to 2D89 for the 999th time, the document that we keep on sending and resending for translation. We've had the final verdict from CLSS. They will not translate anything else. They say the document we have is their final version. So I now say, Your Honours, may we finally have put into e-court the best version that CLSS can produce which is that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I talked to Ms. Korner on a number of occasions about this situation, which is as follows. We submitted the document for an official translation which we did receive. When with the assistance of the OTP we tried to obtain a redacted improved translation from them, we were told that was the best they could produce. For all intents and purposes, the document that Ms. Korner has is a new document. Therefore, we cannot append to an official document a translation of something else. In our view it is not just a technical issue. It is a matter of the exhibit number. Because we had one document and received a translation for it, and the Prosecution sent the same document for translation and got a different translation, so basically we have two different documents now. In the instant case we would have to give to the original document in e-court a translation which isn't official. And it's a problem that I really don't know how to resolve. Perhaps the simplest way would be to attach the translation that Ms. Korner has, but I don't think it's possible in procedural terms, because we have something that is not an official translation of the document in e-court and that's my problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is a problem because over and over again we have sent documents back for revised translation or a new translation. This is exactly what has happened. What the Defence don't like is that CLSS say they can't obtain anything -- they can't translate anything more. So, Your Honours, I do not see there's any difficulty at all. It's the same document. It's got a better translation because there's more of it translated than there was originally, so that is what should happen. I don't personally care procedurally whether we simply put in yet another copy of the original with the revised translation. But it seems to me completely mad because you've got exactly the same original document with one translation that doesn't contain certain words and another translation that does which CLSS said they saw. But one way or another, the time has come to get this revised translation into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if I may add to Ms. Korner's last comment, wouldn't it be adding confusion to have these -- this series of documents in court? Shouldn't -- wouldn't the practical course be to merely look at the last effort by CLSS and forget about the -- the -- what -- the history.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, with respect. And I don't know what Mr. Krgovic's objection is based on because it is happening all the time. All that has to happen is that the Defence upload the new translation instead of the old one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do that. But we received it officially from CLSS so there's no problem. What Ms. Korner is referring to is the document that they received from CLSS upon their request, and when we attached the translation that Ms. Korner received and we send it to CLSS and said, Do this translation, they said, No, this is the official translation, the one that we produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the course we would probably follow is as Ms. Korner has proposed, but we are not formally making a ruling on that now, because it's something that we have to state carefully, both for the benefit of counsel but more particularly for the assistance of the Registry. So it is something that we will probably give an oral ruling about as soon as we settle on the precise language that we should use. Does that cover all of the preliminary matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't know whether we have to waste time on this. We have an e-mail from the Registry about a whole load of documents which, I mean, I cannot see why I have to mention them in open court. They're revised -- go on for pages. But the Registry seems to think we have to make formal applications. These are all -- I can run through them, if you like. But it's just a waste of time, as far as I can see. P63.3 [sic], there was a revised translation because of the translation of the word -- the much vexed word -- okay. I should say 60.3. It's come out differently on the transcript. It has been retranslated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I suggest, Ms. Korner, that rather than, as you say, going through this now, if, as I understand you, there are a number of like documents, wouldn't the simpler course to put this in a omnibus motion and we could deal with it, wouldn't that be the most expeditious way of disposing of all of these matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if necessary, Your Honour, but I mean, I don't understand why it can't just be done? Why does it have to be mentioned in open court? According to the Registry, it has to be mentioned in open court. It's just new translations or the like which have been uploaded, and for the life of me, I can't see why we have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was relieved when Mr. Krgovic had indicated that he wasn't sure how to proceed. I was glad to learn I wasn't the only one. It appears that the simpler course would be, and this is to avoid any error in terms of the -- if they're read out orally and then an error is made in -- particularly dealing with numbers. If the Prosecutor -- if the -- if the Prosecution were to provide a notice with the numbers, and presumably by doing that you would have an opportunity to check the numbers, and the Chamber would then approve it and that would be sufficient notice to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, then we'll just write a notice up with the various numbers. And do Your Honours want to us include 2D89 on this notice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honours, we'll do that. Your Honours, that concludes the matters that I wanted to raise this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, are we done with the housekeeping matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. I said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, those are the matters. I just came to court to deal with exactly the housekeeping matters. So if Your Honours will allow me, I will leave now and Mr. Hannis will deal with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may withdraw now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just before Ms. Korner leaves. I was just -- on page 15, line 11 and 12, Your Honours just said, referring to this 2D89: "... so it is something that we will probably give an oral ruling about as soon as we settle on the precise language that we should use." And I think we need to find out what is the precise language that we should use and then the Trial Chamber should orally rule about that, not that Ms. Korner put that on notice. Because that is not the -- that was not the ruling of the Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is no language to be used. We're saying this is a fuller translation, full stop, and therefore should be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the problem is that there are two translations which are different coming both from the CLSS, so we have to see what is the problem there and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, I'm grateful to Mr. Zecevic for the reminder. And all this means, to my mind, is that the -- we will formulate language to make clear what we are saying about this disputed document and then it would be added to the list of these other documents that are of a like character.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the reason -- Your Honours asked for a list of all the documents where there have been changes for one reason or another which Mr. Smith provided to us and asked us to raise because the Registry had said it had to be mentioned in open court, and on that, obviously, is 2D89, so that will simply be one of the other documents that needs an alteration on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, when I indicated earlier that we would reflect on the language we should use in terms of 2D89, I didn't appreciate that we were faced with -- that -- in the wake of that there would be these other documents that were similarly -- had a similar character.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, again, let's take the simpler course and dispose of this matter, which shouldn't be unnecessarily complicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So would the usher please escort the witness ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Zecevic, do you have any procedural matters before we call the witness in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, none, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I trust that you can hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you're very welcome. Would you be kind enough to read out the solemn declaration that has been handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: First of all, sir, I wish to welcome you to the Tribunal and thank you for coming to give your testimony today. May I, first of all, ask you to state your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Milos Jankovic. I was born on the 30th of October, 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in a village that has two names. Gornji Zabar. And later on it was renamed into Pelagicevo. Up until 1968 it was Gornji Zabar. It is in North-Eastern Bosnia, and the name of the municipality was Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, Mr. Jankovic, may I ask you of your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Jankovic, tell us about your occupation in 1992. What did you do and where did you work? Shortly, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier, and then in 1992, and then throughout 1992, I worked in the public security station in Prijedor. I was head of the communications department and encryption. That is to say, communications that were at the disposal of the police in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Jankovic, we see that you have already been testifying here in this Tribunal in the Stakic case, so I need not run with you again the modes of testimony here. But there is perhaps a bit of information that you would wish to have, and that is the schedules that we have set out for your testimony here. You're being called as a witness by Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, who is sitting there, and you will be examined by his Defence counsel, Mr. Krgovic, whom I believe you have already met. Mr. Krgovic has asked for five hours to complete his examination-in-chief. And Mr. Stanisic, whose counsel is here -- for Mr. Zecevic, has asked for three hours to complete his cross-examination of you. And finally, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting you. I think we have sent the mail, perhaps you haven't received it, but after meeting with the witness yesterday and meeting with Mr. Krgovic, we reassigned the topics, questions, and the time that will be needed, and in that e-mail, we reduced the time that we would need down to a maximum of one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Cvijetic. I was not aware of that. So just to resume, Mr. Jankovic. The Stanisic Defence intends to cross-examine you for a maximum of an hour and a half. And, finally, as I was saying, the Prosecution has asked for eight hours to complete its cross-examination of you. After that, there will be an opportunity for Mr. Krgovic to put further questions to you in his re-direct examination. And during your testimony, the Judges may have questions to you as well. All of this boils down to the fact that we anticipate that we will have to have you with us for all of this week, and we hope that your testimony here can be completed by Friday at the latest. You may recall from your earlier testimony that we run normally sessions of one hour and a half, after which the tapes have to be changed. So we have breaks of 20 minutes every 90 minutes. Mr. Jankovic, all I have left to tell you is that you are now going to testify under oath, and this oath means that you may be prosecuted for false testimony and for perjury, if, during your testimony here, you provide false or incomplete testimony to the Court. And I should also tell you that there is a severe penalty for providing such false or incomplete testimony. Do you have any questions to the Bench before we begin your examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, thank you for this information although I was familiar with most of it. Now, as for how long I would stay here, I came here to do my best, to help as much as I can, so I don't have any special circumstances that would limit my stay. I will stay as long as I need to stay. I don't want to stay for too long, of course, that's natural. But you go ahead, you put your questions, and I will respond. I will tell the truth. And I won't make any mistakes. Of course, these events took place long time ago, so perhaps I will miss this or that, but I'm here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. And we are grateful for your presence. Mr. Jankovic, if at any point you have anything that you wish to raise with the Chamber or the parties, then please do not hesitate to just come forward. Mr. Krgovic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, since the two of us speak the same language and we fully understand each other, I would kindly ask you to make a brief pause before answering my questions so that the interpreters can interpret both my question and your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, tell me, please, what schooling do you have?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after elementary school, I went to secondary school for mechanical technicians for four years, than took me up to 1968, following which I went to the army. I graduated there from the school for reserve officers, and I reached the rank of artillery captain in the JNA. After this military school, which lasted for one year, in 1969, I enrolled into the school of electrical engineering, which I concluded in 1975, becoming the engineer for electrical -- electronics. And following that, I started working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We need to correct something. You graduated from the school of electrical engineering. Which department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Electronics and telecommunications. That's how it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, tell us, please, when did you start working in police?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I started working in 1975 to 1980, I worked in private sector, in a factory. And then in August of 1980, I came to Prijedor, and I remained there until I retired in 2008, somewhere in June. On the 30th of June, 2008. I worked in police force there. So from August of 1980 until June of 2008, I worked continuously in police. Performing always the same tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the title that you had, the exact position that you had from when you started until you retired.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, each police station has its own department for transfer of information, written and verbal, for the needs of the police, as well as encryption of that information. I headed that department. That is to say, that I was responsible for organising work and everything else that needed to be done. I had to ensure that the system worked well. I was responsible for that, and I was responsible for everything that had to do with that system of communications. My superior was chief of the police station. So the person that headed the police station was my superior. And I was responsible to him. I also had specialist responsibilities within my line of work, in the MUP, because there were organisational units at the centre, and the organisation changed from year to year. And sometimes my superior within the specialist line of work was in Sarajevo, and sometimes he was in Banja Luka, and I was responsible to him regarding the technical aspects of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, in answer to His Honour Judge Harhoff's question, you said that you testified in other cases before this Tribunal. Can you tell us which cases were these.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Prcac case. There were others in -- accused in that case but I was called by the Prcac Defence team. It was in 2001, unless I'm mistaken. And the second time I testified was in Dr. Stakic's case, which was sometime in autumn of 2003, I believe. Yes. The first time round was in the spring, in the month of May of 2001; and this was in winter time. It was snowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After having testified in these two cases, were you interviewed by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, much later. I think it was in autumn -- I think it was the month of November of 2007. I was interviewed in Banja Luka for a prolonged period of time. There was a lady and a gentleman there. And I think it lasted for eight hours, the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us on how many occasions did you meet with representatives of Mr. Zupljanin's Defence. When was your first contact?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the summer before last, or late autumn. I know Mr. Vukovic [as interpreted] from our student days. He invited me for a cup of coffee and asked me if I'd be prepared to testify. I said that I would, although I said that everything that I had to say I had already told the Prosecution and in my testimonies before the Tribunal. So I expressed my willingness and we didn't discuss it further. That was our first encounter. The second time was in late December or early January, when you came. It wasn't a long conversation, and you asked me roughly what it was that I would have to say. So I briefly summarised my earlier testimonies. And you said that there was a possibility that I might be called to appear. You asked me if I agreed to it, and I said that I would. I said that I would be prepared to come, but I also said that whatever I had to say, I had already told to the representatives of the Prosecution. I told them everything I knew. And that was that. The next time you called me was sometime during the summer. When was it? It was summer. And it was a brief conversation, where I was told that I would be called to appear shortly before August or, if that would fall through, then it would be sometime in October. I wanted to know precisely when. I live on my own and I often go to Prijedor, Banja Luka, to Posavina, to visit my family. I wanted to know when this would be so that I would be at home. And there was no difficulty there. So you called me - when was it? - just now. I was prepared to come and I came. So, in my view, we met three times, I think. It was that winter, back then, and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Vukelic ask you once you were told and you agreed to be a witness for the Zupljanin Defence, did he ask you if you wanted to talk to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He called me on the phone, late July or August, anyway it was summer. Somebody called me, I don't recall who it was, who said that -- who asked me whether I would be willing to talk to the Prosecution. I believed that I had nothing to tell the Prosecution and I said no. Why? Well, because for eight hours I kept saying everything I knew and I told them everything I had to say, so why would they be speaking to me again? Even before, when I testified in the courtroom I said everything I knew. That would amount to repetition. I didn't find it logical, so I didn't dare to. I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please slow down, because what you just said has not been adequately interpreted. So who was it? Who called you on the phone?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Vukelic did. In the second half of summer. I don't remember the time. He asked me, I don't recall his exact words, that there was a need or that somebody wanted me to speak to the Prosecution and would I be prepared to speak to them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what was your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I gave it a bit of thought, and I recall that back in 2007, as I just said, I gave a very extensive interview to OTP representatives. And they're all Prosecutors to me. I don't make a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So what did you tell Mr. Vukelic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told him that I had told them everything I had to say, that I would merely repeating myself, and I wouldn't want to speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer hasn't been recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Last Friday, when we met here, did I ask you if you had changed your position and would agree to meet with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told you that my position was still the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. This bit is clear. Did you meet with me and somebody else from the Defence team yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was this other gentleman with you. What's his name? This one who I got to know. Your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I meant the meeting that we had yesterday afternoon with me and Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clear that up before we proceed. Mr. Jankovic, I asked you about your employment. Was anyone else from your family employed in the Prijedor public security station in 1991 and before?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a wife and two children. My wife worked in the very same station, and she was charged with white-collar crime. She had a degree in law and had been dealing with white-collar crime all her professional life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, tell us, when did you stop working in Prijedor and start working in Banja Luka; and what were your duties at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't ask me about that, and it may be important, that in March of 1994, because I had a surgery and was on sick-leave, I was away from work in Prijedor, though I continued working from home. And it was on the 1st of November, 2001, that I transferred from Prijedor to Banja Luka and stayed there until my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what were the duties you were charged with?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was only a portion of duties related to communications, i.e., maintenance of equipment and installation of new equipment. It was mostly this strictly technical part, and I was the head of the section dealing with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, we're talking about 1991 -- or, rather, we're talking about 1992. Can you tell us what was - briefly - your line of duty and the tasks you were charged -- charged with in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it 1992 or ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was the same sort of duties I had been charged with before 1992. The communications section that I was the head of had two sets of duties. One was communication operators. What did they do? They received written dispatches, typed them up on those machines, and sent them onto the addressees. They would, likewise receive any incoming dispatches. The dispatches could have been of open type or encrypted. Coded, in other words. That was what they did. Those that were outgoing were being coded and those that were incoming were being decoded and sent to those who they were intended for. This is called the exploitation of the communications system. And you've got three shifts of workers charged with these duties. In other words, there's always someone doing the job. The second set of duties had to do with the installation and repairs of all the equipment ranging from telephony to telegraphy, teleprinters, various other machines. In other words, equipment transmitting written information. Then radio sets of ultra short waves, et cetera. All sorts of ranges, including the portable radio sets that police officers would have on them. My duty was to be present there and take care that all these duties are performed as smoothly as possible, to be of assistance and to supervise everything. If any specific tasks were given to us, I'd be summoned by my superior. I would be responsible for the work of my small unit. I would report on its activities, et cetera. Of course, it had to be carried out in keeping with the rules in force. We had weekly meetings, and, where needed, daily meetings. This was the case in 1992. We had monthly reports, reports every three months, half yearly, and yearly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch what the witness said at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, the interpreters didn't understand what you said at the end. But you said here - I have a correction to make - that the meetings were weekly and daily meetings and then you mentioned 1992. It says that you said that this was the case in 1992, but what did you say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me correct myself. The reporting rules were the same back in 1990 and in 1992. However, the rules were not adhered to in 1992. Thus, for instance, at times it was obligatory for us to hold morning -- the morning briefings, where we superiors would be duty-bound to report on our activities. And then it would so happen that they would tell us that the meeting would not be held and, of course, then nobody could be informed about the results of our work. I think I've made myself quite clear now, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will get back to that later. It was just something that I wanted to have corrected in the transcript. Mr. Jankovic, after the multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did there come a change in the leadership structure of the public security station in Prijedor; and, if so, what was it about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When multi-party elections were held, elsewhere, as well as in our area, parties were supposed to have a bearing on the composition of the leadership structure. Only two important issues were at stake, i.e., chief of the station; and police commander. The police commander comes under the chief of the station within the hierarchy. There were similar cases in our municipalities as well, but I was able to see what was going on in our municipality. Negotiations were going on and on, and they simply weren't able to come to an agreement as to who would occupy each post. As far as I remember now, an agreement was reached among these parties elsewhere and in our areas as well, that the party that was victorious in the elections would be the one appointing the chief of the station; whereas, the party that won -- that was the runner-up, let's say, would be the one appointing the commander. So the same was true for the local authorities. The party that won the elections would appoint the president of the municipality, and the runner-up would appoint the chairman of the Executive Board, the one that won the votes right after the first one. That was how Hasan Talundzic came to be our chief of the station. Dusan Jankovic became the commander. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, did you retain the same post?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any alterations within the SJB? Were people transferred to other jobs as a result of the agreement between the parties with regard to the functioning of the station?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were shifts like that. For example, the station commander was Fikret Kadiric, and now, since Dusan Jankovic assumed his post, he was moved to the position of the commander of the traffic police. That's just one example. I don't remember, but there were similar examples like this one. It is the prerogative of a chief to move people around. The first thing they always do is that they change their secretary, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jankovic, before Hasan Talundzic, who had been the chief of the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: For a brief time, it was Slobodan Stojanovic. Sead Besic was also there, but also for a relatively short period of time, and then he was succeeded by Slobodan Stojanovic, and Besic went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was the nationality of Slobodan Stojanovic who was replaced by Hasan Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb. I don't know how he declared himself officially, but according, and judging by his name, he must have been a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about Hasan Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see this is a time for the break. Can we do that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. And we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, let us resume where we left off. Apart from the building where the public security station of Prijedor -- where the uniformed police were, were there any -- any branch offices or detached offices that were not housed in the building of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were. There was a police station of Ljubija. There was a Kozarac police section, and I think that in Omarska, there used to be sometimes a section, sometimes a station. Anyway it was in Ljubija, Kozarac, and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were they part of the communications system of the SJB Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They had an outer short-wave radio set, a stationary one, located at the station. They had a telephone line as well. But they didn't have any teleprinter communication lines for the exchange of written information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to the Prijedor SJB, did your service maintain communications systems in some other public security stations; and did you have any ties with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. According to the organisation chart, the Prijedor covered Sanski Most, the then-called Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica, as was also called like this at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about communication, what was the relationship within your centre and their respective centres? Did you have some kind of superior role over them? How did this all function? Can you please explain the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning communications itself, we were superior to them. However, when it came to organising day-to-day work, they were independent from us, and they had ties with the CSB Banja Luka. So from the overall aspect of the police, they were under the CSB of Banja Luka. However, in the domain of the communications, due to the technical aspects of the system, they had to be connected, first, with Prijedor, and via Prijedor, with Banja Luka, and further on with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us, after the multi-party elections and the appointment of the new leadership, were there any changes in the way in which the station was managed, in the way how communication operated, and how jobs were performed? I'm talking about the period when the new leadership came that was nominated by the winning parties.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: There were changes. Technically speaking, those changes were not significant because the devices that we had continued to operate in the way they used to. However, as one by one broke down, conditions changed. Now, as for the organisation aspect, huge changes occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain to us what you just said? How did it reflect on your work; and can you give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: For example, in the previous normal course of work, I wasn't authorised for many things within my purview, and I wasn't able to take independent decisions concerning communications. Instead, I had to address my supervisor. For example, if we're talking about a procurement of a new piece of equipment, I would go to my supervisor, he would explore the possibility, approve it, or disapprove it, and the work would go on. Now, when Hasan Talundzic came, who had no other experience with the police other than when he was stopped by drink driving, it turned out that he virtually had no knowledge about our work, and I didn't feel the need to ask him anything, which left me with a void upwards. I couldn't cooperate with anyone. I could only function downwards. I could cooperate only with the people who were subordinate to me. All of a sudden, this line of communication was lost. That's just one of the examples. I can give you many more. Or -- the existing question -- function was jeopardised, and a new one was not put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, after the multi-party elections, and after the appointment of new executives, was there any influence from the local party vis-a-vis the managing and running of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. That was the only connection. Hasan Talundzic was appointed by the SDA. He knew them, they were the ones who appointed them. Supposedly he was reporting to them, given that they had appointed me. I didn't pay too much attention to him, but it was easy to notice that if he would receive a significant dispatch, he would take this piece of paper and go across the road to the president of the municipality or whoever for consultations. In our previous work, once the chief of police received a dispatch, he either consult his co-workers or his superior centre, i.e., the superior officer according to the chain of command. Now the situation was different. And there were many similar examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, at that time, who was the president of the municipality, who was the president of the SDA in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: When the parties took over power, the winning party in Prijedor was the SDA. The president of the municipality was a high school teacher. I think he was called Muhamed Cehajic. He was the professor of the Serbian language. The president of the SDA was Dr. Mirza Mujadzic. That's as far as the SDA was concerned. Now, so far as the SDS was concerned, Dr. Mico Kovacevic was the Chairman of the Executive Board and our commander was Dusan Jankovic. And, as I said, the chief was Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the SDS president in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, listen, I was never a member of the party and I didn't follow that. I think that Simo Miskovic was the one, but I'm not sure about that. Whether it was somebody else I don't know. I wasn't a member, I didn't read the papers, I didn't attend any meetings, but I think that he was in that post for a period of time during 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about this subject, were you a member of any other political party after the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, never. I had been a member of the League of Communists, but one had to be because it was impossible to get a job if you were not a member. Everybody was there. However, after the elections, to this date, I never became a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the League of Communists until when?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Until they disintegrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, with the outbreak of war in Croatia and when the ethnic divisions emerged in Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell me whether all these tensions and all these situations had any impact on the overall operation of the SJB in Prijedor? I'm talking about the end of 1991 and the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It started immediately, from the moment when the parties were formed and when they seized power, what emerged is something that is called by single term tensions. But in my view, it was a terribly complicated process. You would hear some unpleasant stories on a daily basis. So you would hear bad things coming from one nation, and the other nation would hear bad things coming from the first nation, et cetera. So all these confrontations were piling up, and ultimately, for example, I myself and other two people were not directly involved in this. There was an inspector for economic crime working together with my wife, and we were on very good terms. All of a sudden he started avoiding me. Yes, he would say good morning or good afternoon, but if could -- he couldn't help it, he would try to avoid having any further contact with me, of having coffee with me and things like that. So all of this was felt outside of the station as well. One could feel that in the town itself. Admittedly, there were people who did not react in that same way. For example, I had a colleague from the college and we maintained good relations but that was not always the case. Now, I can give you numerous examples of how these things that in the previous period were not normal were now happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, tell us, did there exist within the Prijedor public security station members of the reserve force; and was there a reserve police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a reserve police station there, when I got there, from before. The municipality of Prijedor had 43, I believe, local communes, and each of these had their own reserve police station. And this was true for the municipalities in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, before you move on, could I ask the witness. Mr. Witness, you gave the example -- in your previous answer you gave the example about the -- your relation with the inspector of economic crime. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ago was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What name did you mention? Ago? Ago who? What was his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ago Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ago Sadikovic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you that we were quite close. I socialised with him more than I did with others. We would frequently have a cup of coffee, but that was before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And he stayed in the force until when; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the 30th of April, you know the story of the 30th of April, when the Serbs got in in the morning, those who gained access to the SUP asked that an oath be taken, as had been the case before, that they would discharge the duties of the SUP, but this was required of everyone, not just the Muslims, including myself. So you would take an oath and place your signature in this book that they had, and whoever did so was allowed to proceed to their work post. And so I did. Those who refused to had to give back their police ID and their fire-arm. All of us had pistols at the time. And then the individual was free to go where they wished to. This is how things happened on the first morning. There were Muslims who signed the oath, but there were also those who refused to do so. Over time, they somehow separated in terms of the fact that the Serbs who had refused to sign the oath initially, probably because they needed the salary, returned to their work post and were reinstated, whereas Muslims left the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want to confine my question to this acquaintance of yours, Ago Sadikovic. Is that how Ago Sadikovic left the force, on or about the 30th of April, 1992? Was he one of them who didn't want to sign the state -- the oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No, he wasn't. He didn't state -- well, there was this other inspector whom I knew well as well. Why? Because they worked with my wife. They were upstairs from me, a couple of offices away. I wasn't familiar with all the people working at the station, but I was familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So just to make your answer totally clear, because there is a yes and a no in the answer. If I understood you well, you said he, I mean Ago, did not sign or give the oath, and therefore left the force. Is that right? A yes or a no will suffice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is true is that Ago did not sign the oath that morning, and I never saw him again, either on the day or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, let me follow up on what His Honour Judge Delvoie asked you about. You said that there were Muslims who initially signed the oath and then you went on to say something else. Can you tell us, when it comes to signing the oath, were there cases where those who initially signed the oath later on retracted it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Enes, I don't know what his name was, he worked with my wife. He stayed on for a couple of days only. I didn't talk to him or anyone else, so I don't know why it was that he ultimately left. And, finally, Mirsad Cahuric [phoen] was a communications officer, and I was his supervisor; also a Muslim. He was a good worker. That was my view of him. And a good man. I tried to the best of my ability to make it as comfortable for him to stay in that environment as possible. He did stay on for perhaps a month or a month and a half, but then he left as well. Of his own will. Nobody chased him away. As far as I know, he was the last Muslim to leave in that period of time. At a later date some of those returned, but he was the last Muslim to leave our station. I tried as best I could to help him. There were these other colleagues and I as well who helped him get food supplies, because they were people who did not dare to walk about the town. I didn't go later on to see for myself how he was doing, because I know he had two children, but I did send these colleagues of mine to bring him food supplies and see that he is doing well. So I hope I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that he left a month and a half later. What -- did he leave of his own free will? Because that's one bit that is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did leave voluntarily and never told me why. I did speak to him later, but we spoke of neutral things, as it were. I didn't want to ask him about it. But I can tell you what my assumption is. At the time, various international organisations started transporting people in an organised fashion to elsewhere in Europe, and I'm talking about entire families. So I suppose he felt it would be better for him to go elsewhere in Europe and get out of the area where there was a war brewing. So he was lucky enough to have his wife and his children board one of the convoys and leave for Germany. He, on the other hand, was taken on by the Muslims, and I know that he continued in the same line of work in the police station in Travnik. He came back later. He is now in Bosanski Novi -- he is now in Sanski Most, and I do see him occasionally, when our duties permit us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, let us go back to the issue of the reserve police stations. What was the ethnic makeup of these reserve police stations compared to the local communes that they covered? Would the makeup correspond to the ethnic composition of the local communes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had somewhat more knowledge of these issues. Why was this? There was a programme in place of instruction and training for various subjects, including communications. That was where I came in. And I would be holding these training sessions. That's how I came to know people from various stations. The ethnic composition of these stations corresponded to the ethnic makeup of the population inhabiting a given local commune, and they had to have high moral integrity, and they had to be individuals who had no previous criminal record. They were also people who were not prone to drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1992 - and I'm talking about March and April - how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you that this wasn't strictly my line of work, but in some of the meetings that I attended, I came to learn that we - and when I say "we," I mean Prijedor - had 700 individuals and 450 rifles, so there was talk of the shortage of rifles. I don't know if this can provide some sort of an approximation of these figures. I wasn't privy to any other information in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, tell us, did there exist a special department in the public security station in Prijedor that dealt with the reserve police force; and, if so, who headed the department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that there was always one work post set aside for these duties. At the time, it was Muharem Ceric who was the incumbent on that post. I know because his office was just next to mine, and I would see these commanders coming to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in the period between early 1992 and the outbreak of conflicts in Prijedor, were there any changes in the personnel? You talked about the pre-war period, but was it also the case in this period leading up to the outbreak of conflicts? Was this principle respected?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. Well, first of all, let me tell you that I wasn't one of those who would be checking these people, but I did hear stories to the effect that Ceric was admitting criminals onto the force. When they said "criminals," perhaps they didn't mean criminals in that strict sense of the word but perhaps that they were not the best of individuals for those posts, in view of their earlier activities. And, as I saw these criminals, I could tell by their names that they were some sort of -- well, perhaps it wasn't the case but that's what it looked like, a Muslim name and a man of suspicious past. There were such individuals. These were stories that I heard from those who were better placed to know these things. As for myself, I wasn't either familiar with criminals, nor did I have these lists of all these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us what, roughly, was the head count of that particular police department, whatever it is called, in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 10 to 15. I don't think there were any -- that there were more than 20 or less than 10 of them at any point in time. I know what the area was under their control, and I believe that this was roughly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about members of the reserve force there as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm referring to active-duty policemen only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether mobilisation was effected at any point of time of the reserve force in the sense that they were issued uniforms and weapons, and that these stations became active?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, speaking about the events of March and April 1992, were there any visits from Sarajevo by officials who came to Prijedor? How often did that take place, and do you know what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were instances like that. I know that a few days before, or better still, in the second half of April to be more precise, a few - I don't know how many because I know for -- about at least two or three -- Avdo Hebib used to come quite often from Sarajevo. I don't know exactly, but I think he was an under-secretary for public security. In the MUP organisation, he would be person number three. You had a minister, you had his deputy, and then the chief of public security deputy. Now, this one was the chief of public security department. In the previous period, such a high-ranking MUP official would visit Prijedor once in a few years only. Now, this one came three times within the span of ten days. I personally had no dealings with him. I don't know what he talked about, but I do know that if I went to Hasan Talundzic, my chief, to consult him, the secretary would tell me, You cannot go in. Mr. Hebib is inside. Well, I thought to myself, he was here yesterday or the day before, and that's all that I knew. I don't know what they discussed, what subjects they talked about, nothing. But I did conclude that something was out of order for him to come so often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us whether, in that period, which is early 1992, was there any gathering people around their ethnic backgrounds? Were there any communications between people of the same ethnicity on various matters?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. For example, in the past, all the agreements used to reach at what we used to call the senior executive staff meetings. We would coordinate and agree on what had to be done, when it had to be done, et cetera. Now these meetings were few and far apart, and even if they did happen, the topics addressed at these meetings were almost insignificant. I also noticed that the Ago that I mentioned before, who was in the office next to my wife's, and that is three or four offices away from my office, I saw Commander Fikret Kadiric and Hasan Talundzic coming to Ago very frequently. Even if you don't pay particular attention you just cannot help noticing it. I don't know why these people were flocking together and what they were talking about. But I can tell that you the same practice was pursued on the Serbian side, but I myself was not part of the police, so I didn't have anyone who was close enough to me to do that. I didn't interfere in anyone's job, and they left me alone basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us do you know of any examples of people being armed - I'm talking about the civilians, be it the Muslims or the Serbs - in the early spring of 1992? Do you know anything about that? Do you know that the process of arming ordinary citizens began in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it did. You didn't have to be particularly a proper sleuth in order to detect that. First of all, let me tell you, there was fighting already going on in Slavonia and I think that in Prijedor, in the town square, one could buy a hand-grenade. I don't know how it costs. I think it was 10 or 20 German marks. So these were available for purchase on the street. Then gun-fire began, which wasn't the case before, and I don't know who was shooting or why. Then I heard - I don't know how I heard of it actually - there was Slivko Titkovic [phoen] from Kozarusa. He was a Ukrainian and Kozarusa was a Muslim village. He heard and he told me that in a number of restaurants there, people were getting together and rifles were being distributed. Something of the sort. I don't know. I cannot say that this was reliable information. I didn't take them to be so, but I don't also think that it was all the product of their imagination. There was shooting for a fact. I didn't know the extent of it, but it did exist. I once went to Kozarac in April as part of my duty, and the people in Kozarac did not even try to conceal from me that they had communication devices that were operative. They were leftovers from 1984 Winter Olympics in Sarajevo. Now, this Kozara section of the police had these devices. I was familiar with them, because that's my profession. I asked them how did they get hold of this, and they said, Chief Hasan had brought it from Sarajevo. Never before. Not a single communication device had arrived Prijedor without me knowing about it. Because it was such a very professional and technical thing that it was never the case that the chief would bring such devices himself because they were coming from different professions. But if you look at this minute detail, it speaks for itself that a process was underway of separating functions. Why were these devices procured without me being involved in that? It wasn't a big deal, but it did happen. So these things were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
