utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us are you acquainted with Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, and if you are, for how long?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have known him for quite a long time, but I don't know him well. I know him from our student days. That was back in 1973 or 1974. We were residing in the dormitory, but we attended different faculties. Therefore, we were not close. So this was when I first got acquainted with him. After we'd finished school, I worked, and I told you where I worked; whereas, he was working with the Banja Luka police. Our paths never crossed in terms of our careers. I never saw him before. I heard of him through the line of work. And then, later on, I don't know exactly when, but I think when the multi-party elections were held, I know that he was appointed chief of the centre, and, of course, as a result, I found him to be more interesting as such, if I may say so. But, again, I didn't have any direct contacts with him because he was the second rung on this ladder, so he was above my chief according to the chain of command, and as for professional line, he was the chief of Rako Dragovic. Therefore, I didn't have any need to communicate directly with him. But I knew him, as I said, and we would just greet each other if we happened to come across one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, in 1992, in Prijedor, did you have an opportunity to see Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was when this meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Jankovic. Let me just ask you a question. Do you recall approximately in which month this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I know the exact date. As for this date, I know it exactly because of the piece of paper that I still have at home, and it was held on 9th of April, 1992. I somehow happened to keep this piece of paper, and it's written on it. So shall I tell you about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us just make some kind of introduction. On the 9th of April, 1992, you saw Stojan Zupljanin in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us where you were on that day and what were the circumstances of what you did when you arrived at the station.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that in my testimony in the Stakic case, and -- but I'm now going to repeat it now. On the 9th of April, 1992, on the morning of that day, I heard that Chief Zupljanin was expected to come to Prijedor. Of course, this is news if a chief is coming to Prijedor. However, I heard that he was not going to come to the station but that he would first go to the municipality in order to consult with the municipal leadership in order to reduce the tensions, if possible. Now, as I said, he was two levels above me within the hierarchy. I presume that if he were to come to the station, my chief might call me. However, since he was not coming to us, he was, rather, going to the municipality, I didn't think it was of any significance and I went to Bosanski Novi for an assignment in the company of one of our technicians. I returned at around 1400. I cannot be very precise. It's half an hour, give and take. When I returned, I noticed that the situation was not normal. This whole region -- and if you are familiar with the town of Prijedor, you would know that there is a small park in front of the municipal building. After that, there is a bigger park, and, roughly speaking, this is an area which extends for some 150 metres, and behind the police station there was a court-house and also a small park. Now, this whole area was covered with scattered group of youngsters in civilian clothes, people of the ages of 19 or 20. They didn't have any weapons but they all were dressed in jackets although it wasn't very cold and they all had their hands in their pockets. They were scattered around in groups of five or six each. So the distance between myself and that area was some 10 or 15 metres. And I thought there was something wrong about it, but it did attract my attention. I didn't scrutinise it too closely. I went back to my communications centre and my office. I asked the duty officer what was going on, and he said, I don't know. In our building there was an unusually small number of people. You hardly could see anyone in the halls. When I went to my wife's office, who was the inspector for economic crime, I asked her, What's this? She was busy working on some file. She didn't know anything. This caused some kind of concern in me, but in order to be too conspicuous I asked her to join me so that we could go out and make a circle around this park so that we can see all those groups. She took me by the arm and we walked together. I managed to count roughly some 10 or 12 groups, times three to five, or ten, so that would make approximately 400 people, and that's a lot of people. After that, I got back, and when I was at the door of my office and I said that Muharem Ceric's office was next to mine, who I said was in charge of the reserve police, I saw that moment three men emerging from his office one after another. They were whispering and all they -- I heard them saying was, Just go slowly, one by one. That was all. I entered my office and I saw the three men through my window going from one group to another and telling them something. There was something going on, and I didn't know what it was. So I went to the chief's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Pause there, Mr. Jankovic. Can you tell us, first, what was the ethnicity of the individuals who were coming out of the office next door?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to tell what their ethnicity was. I know what Ceric's ethnicity was, but not of the three that I didn't know. I saw them come out of the office one by one. And then out of the window I was able to see them working the various groups of people, going from one to the next and telling them something. I was telling you that I went downstairs in the direction of the chief's office. In the centre, you had the secretary's office. To the right, was the office of the chief. And to the left was the office of the head of the crime police. He was called Bajo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His nickname was Bajo. So I asked, Bajo, what's going on? Who are these people gathering around here? He said he didn't know. A couple of minutes later, the secretary popped her head round the door and said, Milos, she meant Bajo, do not leave the premises because the chief has just told me that a meeting will be held in his office, and Chief Zupljanin will be there. So, in fact, we stayed there for some 10 or 15 minutes more, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what the name of Bajo was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Ranko Mijic, also known as Bajo. That is how we referred to him. But his name was Ranko Mijic. And, in fact, Chief Talundzic did come. We went to his office, and Talundzic addressed the secretary Mira, as he stepped into the office and told her Miro -- Mira, if somebody should be looking after me, please, I am unavailable. We don't want to be interrupted. Let me first tell you that I was caught quite unprepared. I didn't have a notebook with me or anything. I wasn't ready for the meeting. I would normally have at least a sheet of paper and a pen to make notes. Anyway, I managed to get hold of this sheet of paper which read -- and this is something that I found later on after the war because I always kept these pieces of paper that I would have, and that's why I can tell you this clearly because I still have this sheet of paper which reads: It was the 9th of April, 1992, and the meeting was attended by --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Jankovic. But I'm just about to show a document on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Great, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 65 ter 00029D2 in e-court. That's in the Zupljanin Defence binder, number 6. And I'll give you a hard copy. Can I have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you should consult what you have before you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't really read what the screen shows, the monitor. I prefer to look at the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, please, look at the date.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The paper reads the 9th of April, 1992. And it's my handwriting. Shall I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says: Chief of centre --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just note for the rest who are listening to me that this may be a sort of professional deformation of mine. You see, when I make notes on these little pieces of paper, they are intended solely for myself, and it's just the backbone of an event. It's the skeleton. And that's why the text is very curt, perhaps, to some, meaningless. But I can tell you exactly whey meant by what I noted here. So let me clarify for you what it is that I jotted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read the title, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: So what I wrote up there is the date. Chief of centre. And meeting. In other words, meeting with the chief of centre. Beneath it, it reads main or basic agreement. Well, that's not what it was but that was what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you go through the various names and tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I will. And as I said, this was just an abbreviated way of making notes. Stole stands for Mr. Zupljanin. Hasan stands for Hasan Talundzic, the chief. Dule --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just slow down, please, for the sake of interpreters and the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat: Stole stands for Stojan Zupljanin. Hasan is the chief of the station, Hasan Talundzic. Dule is short for Dusan Jankovic, the then-commander. Kecan, that's the last name, Radovan Kecan, assistant commander for crime within the station. Ziko stands for Zijad Basic, again, assistant commander, but he was charged with a different line of duty. I don't know which exactly. Fikret stands for Fikret Kadiric --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Fikret Kadiric was commander of traffic police at the time, I believe. Djuro, that was Djuro Prpos. I think he was Fikret's deputy at the time. He was traffic and transport engineer by profession. Next to Djuro is Mijic, which is the Ranko Mijic I was referring to. Then there's me and the chief of public security. I didn't know the man before. Jahic or Jehic, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So Bajazit Jahic, he was what?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It says "JB" meaning chief of public security --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Of which institution was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In my understanding of the structure at the time, he was the chief for the overall public security, including us, and he was the one who was immediately subordinate to Mr. Zupljanin. There was him and the chief of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So chief of public security of the Security Services Centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that's convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We would take a break and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We reconvene for this last session under Rule 15 bis; Judge Delvoie being absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 2 -- or rather, 65 ter 000292D. Can we have it on our screens again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did we break off?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back to Mr. Bajazit Jahic, because his first name wasn't in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, his first and last name tell us that he is a Muslim. I don't know how he declared himself to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jankovic, were all these individuals whose names you jotted down here present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was writing their names as I was looking at them. I could not have made a mistake. The meeting began, and I jotted it down, like this. It was a habit of mine. This particular meeting was no different from others that I attended. It was simply a lifetime's habit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please ask to you read what we can see here in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. The meeting began. Hasan Talundzic, the chief of our station, opened the meeting. He announced that the chief, Mr. Zupljanin, would take the floor, which he did. In this opening address of his --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jankovic. Can we clarify one thing. You said that Mr. Zupljanin was supposed to come to the meeting in the municipal building; whereas, he came to the meeting in the SUP. So what became of that meeting in the municipality, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As we're discussing this, the way I jotted it down here, I didn't know why he was there. What I heard before from -- or, rather, what I heard from my colleagues later was that this other meeting of his did not take place so he came to meet with us. It didn't sound illogical to me. But this is what I heard, that the other meeting was not held. But these were unofficial sources. It -- it was something that I heard in the grape-vine. It doesn't necessarily follow that it was the truth. He wanted to hold the meeting because of the heightened tensions. And of all those various stories I heard, I only remember the gist of it, i.e., that he wanted to have a meeting in the municipal building with the leaders of the SDA, i.e., president of the SDA, Mirza Mujadzic, chief of the municipality, Cehajic, and other important figures, with a view to easing interethnic intentions in the municipality of Prijedor. That was my understanding of his visit. Apparently he had not been received because -- well, let me tell that you both he and Mr. Bajazit had civilian clothes. His driver apparently had a uniform and a short-barrelled weapon, let's say it was a pistol, and apparently this was the reason why these people wouldn't receive him. That was the story about the town. I don't know if it was the truth or not. At any rate, he came to the police building and we had this meeting with him. Another thing that I heard from these stories was that he did not go back to Banja Luka taking the direct road but, rather, he took a detour via Dubica because he was afraid of what might happen in Kozarac. So, again, this is something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say what was the town he went through by way of detour?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Dubica. You have a 50-kilometre road between Prijedor and Banja Luka. Instead he took the road to Dubica, that was 30 kilometres, then Gradiska, and then from there it took him another 15 -- 50 kilometres to Banja Luka. So basically it was twice the length of the direct road, but apparently there was talk of barricades or roadblocks having been erected in Kozarac. I don't know if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, is it customary for the president of a municipality or any other municipal official to refuse to meet up with a chief of a station simply because the person who was his escort carried a pistol?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That was non-sensical. Let me say, first of all, that even in peacetime, chiefs of centre would be driven about by a policeman. So the individual wasn't just a driver. He was also a policeman and a body-guard. And, of course, being what he was, such a policeman would have a uniform and a fire-arm. I mean, really, what sort of a policeman would it have been without a fire-arm? It wasn't a submachine-gun or anything of the sort. It was a pistol which was issued to police officers by their establishment or position. I'm not speaking specifically about his driver because I didn't see him on that day, but I'm speaking from my experience about drivers who as policemen would have a uniform and a pistol, and that's all. And it was no excuse. In peacetime, when everything was completely calm, the chief was always driven by a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I interrupted you. Would you please go back to reading the document.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So I marked this with a 1 because that was the topic. So under 1, I wrote down Stole said and Hasan said that it is best here. The chief spoke about the organisation of the war time police units exactly as they were defined in the regulations and so on, and he knew to what extent that was respected or not, and he spoke in general terms what needed to be improved, not only in relation to Prijedor but also all other police stations because that was the situation then. Everybody had police stations. And then I wrote Haso speaks about reserve formations. He wants weapons. Stole said that the transformation was needed. This does not accurately reflect it. But it boiled down to the situation that the chief of the station Hasan, or Haso, was saying, I know, Chief, everything is going well with us. We have no such problems. We have resolved all of that. Because the chief of the centre was not saying, In your station this and this is wrong. No. He was speaking in general terms. So Hasan said to him, Everything is going well here. We have resolved all of these issues. I'm stopping down for the sake of interpreters. And then Hasan says, But we need weapons. We have no rifles, Chief. And then he comes up with 700 people and 450 rifles. These numbers have stuck in my head from those times. So 450 rifles and 700 men. Chief Zupljanin spoke about that, saying, Well, gentlemen, why do you need all these rifles? We are public security. We are in charge of law and order. We work with people. Who are we going to fire at with 700 rifles? Are we going to fire at the people with 700 rifles? So that was the gist of his discussion. It wasn't as brief as I conveyed it to you, but that was what he spoke of. He -- I wrote down his words. He said: That's militarisation. We are turning police into army and we cannot do that. We need to organise ourselves in such a way as to persevere in this multinational environment without a conflict. With ensuring that there as few conflicts as possible, that they're as risky [as interpreted] as possible. So that was the gist of his discussion. Of course, not as briefly as I put it to you, but that's what he was saying. And the discussion took much longer than what I have told you here, but that's what they essentially spoke of. And then they moved to another topic. I wrote down here: Transformation of the MUP and establishment of the CSB. And then it is written down here: Stole spoke about the transformation of the MUP. I'm against splitting up of the service. This is what the chief said, and this is what I wrote down. Haso and Fikret do not want the badges. That's what I wrote down, but I will now explain to you what it was about. At the time the Prijedor station, the name kept changing. It used to be a station, and then it was the centre. But at the time it was the public security station that belonged to the centre in Banja Luka. That's how it was in this particular period of time. So, at that time, the station in Prijedor belonged to the centre in Banja Luka. There was a situation at a higher level, and I'm not going to go into that because I'm not all that familiar with it, but they -- there was this organisation of the part of the SUP organised by the Serbs in municipalities with the majority of Serbian population in the area of Bosnian Krajina and that was the jurisdiction of the Banja Luka centre. I forgot which municipalities fell under them, but that's how it was. And in the context in that organisation at a higher level a decision was made that the police representing these persons that I have just mentioned, conditionally speaking, Serbian municipalities, they weren't really Serbian, but that's how I put it. But it was decided that they should have their own insignia, and according to somebody's proposal, they were supposed to have a badge in the shape of a Serbian flag with three colours, red, blue, and white. So -- and the flag was not in a rectangular shape. It was a modified rectangle. Somebody brought a prototype of that badge to show what it would look like, and I think that the chief didn't even take the badge for himself. He gave to Zijad Basic and he said jokingly, Your wife is a Serb, so why don't you take this badge for yourself. I think that that's how it was. This is what I seem to have remembered. It says here Fikret and Hasan. They spoke the most. They were chief and commander of the police station. They said that they wouldn't take those badges. They concluded -- the chief said, Well, I understand what you're saying. We will see what we are going to do with Prijedor and Kotor Varos. These are the municipalities that did not have the majority of Serb population, and he said, We will see what will be decided. You don't have to wear these badges. We will see what solution will be adopted at the political level. We will resolve this. Don't you worry. We shouldn't turn this into a huge problem. Why don't you find an agreement amongst yourself to make sure that our basic work is taken care of, our basic tasks, which was to reduce the interethnic tensions, which were escalating. That was my understanding. And I understood that he had come precisely for that reason, to have that meeting at the municipality. And then, in the continuation, we see I spoke about the concrete agreement for us to be united. Well, this sentence also sounds a bit illogical but it was me who took the floor at this point and I said to them, Listen, people, we can't achieve anything if in one office we have three Muslims sitting and whispering amongst themselves and in the other office we have three Serbs sitting and whispering to themselves. We need to get together and speak openly, and that's the only way we can resolve things. We should not go and isolate ourselves in little groups. So this entire meeting what I wrote down lasted perhaps for an hour. Shall I continue? And then all of a sudden, so we were discussing this, and all of a sudden a secretary showed up at the door saying, Chief, you are urgently needed by Osmet Didovic who was the commander of the police station in Kozarac. And the chief said, Well, tell him to wait. I'm busy now. And then she said, It's urgent. Immediately, please. So we stayed in the room and the chief went out of the room to take care of this. He didn't stay away for long time. Hasan came back and said, Listen, people, the situation is quite complex. People from Kozarac are moving in the direction of Prijedor. I forgot how he described the group, but the idea was that they were about to come to Prijedor, and Osman came, allegedly, to talk to him about what needed to be done. And people were getting a little bit apprehensive, I mean us who were there at the meeting. And immediately we switched the topic. We started talking about what should we do urgently to calm tensions down. So the chief was there, the other two, chief of the station, Fikret was quite actively engaged in everything that was happening. And they concluded that they needed to call urgently two journalists. One from a local radio station and the other one from the local newspaper, "Kozarski Vjesnik." They were to be told to write immediately a proclamation and to broadcast it to calm the residents down, telling them that the police had the situation under control, that nothing bad would happen, nobody was going to attack anyone, that people should not be afraid, that they should stay calmly in their homes, that everything was under control, and that everything would turn out fine. So they called these two journalists, who arrived promptly. I know one of them for sure, because he used to be a neighbour of mine, lived in the building next to me. His name was Nezirevic. He was a Muslim and he was to represent the Muslim population. The other journalist is somebody I didn't know from before, somebody said that his name was Milos Aprilski. I don't really the man, but it was a short person with a round head and short hair. So our leaders, chief of the station, chief of the centre, told them what they needed to do, these journalists, that they didn't spend much time telling them. It wasn't in the nature of giving orders. They didn't really tell them, You have to do this, this and that. No. They said -- they explained the situation. They said, You're a journalist so why don't you write this up and let's broadcast it to make sure that peace is preserved. I did not hear this proclamation on the radio, but later on I heard that it really had a positive effect. In the end I don't know whether these Osmet brought these people or not. At any rate, there were no conflicts, no clashes that day in the afternoon. I heard that the chief went home after that, but not -- not taking the shortest road, rather, taking a detour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a concern, because the answers the witness has given about what the notes supposedly says in some places certainly doesn't match what is in the current English translation. So either we need to do something about revising the translation or going through with the witness word by word, line by line, to see where it differs. Because it was difficult to tell sometimes when he was giving his answer whether he was expanding, now having his memory refreshed by seeing his note from April 1992, or if he was reading literally from the note. And that's my only concern about marking this as an exhibit at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But the -- if we have the note, and when the time comes to understand what the note is about, the -- even if the -- what -- what the answers were to the questions was an expansion or explanation, isn't that -- doesn't that resolve your concern, Mr. Hannis? In other words, it would be not unlike many exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, just a simple example. At line -- at page 52, line 19, he was asked to read the title. And he says: Chief of centre. And: Meeting. The English translation says: Chief of the centre and others. That's just the first example. When we get down further into the body of the text, there's some substantial differences. He mentions that Mr. Zupljanin talked about this would be "militarisation." I don't see that word anywhere in the note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is there, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He explained he a special procedure in making these notes and sometimes using obscure abbreviations that only he would understand. And that's the trouble. The translator translating this doesn't know his secret code or terminology for some things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we have the benefit of the answers that he has given. And, of course, you can explore this in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour, but in that regard, then I guess I would ask that it be MFI'd until I've had a chance to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's a question of translation because the witness read everything out accurately. We can see it in the original. The word "militarisation" is there, as well as the heading: The chiefs of centres and others. Perhaps we should let the witness read this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this is his document so we should have him read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. That would appear to be the simpler course because although we have had the benefit of the -- I was going to say isolated answers you have given to specific questions, bearing in mind that a requirement for admissibility is that the document is one of the languages of the Tribunal, the practical difficulty here is that we see from the English version which has been submitted the difficulties that the interpreters would have had. So we would give the document an exhibit number but take you up on your suggestion to have the witness read it in its entirety. It isn't that long a document so that shouldn't take any length of time. So we'll admit it and mark it, and then the witness can read the -- his original notes and we'll hear what the interpreters say.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Exhibit 2D156. Thank you. I apologise, 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you heard this. Can you please slowly read this document out loud, without any comments whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it. But before that, or after that, I would like to say something. Now I'm going to start reading. 9th April 1992. Yes, it is easier to read from the paper. 9th April 1992. Chief of centre and others. GL agreement. GL stands for main. Stole, Hasan, Dule --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please slowly. Word by word.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Here we go. Main agreement, Stole, Hasan, Dule, Kecan, Ziko, Stole, Hasan. What are they waiting for? Hasan, Dule, Kecan, Ziko, Fikret. Yes, but the screen is not reflecting what I'm saying. That's why I'm looking at it, and it is confusing me. Okay. Ziko, Fikret, Djuro Mijic. Mijic. Now, Mijic, myself, and chief of JB, of public security, (Bajazit) Jehic or Jahic. I'm not sure of that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Number 1, Stole said as for RJM and Haso said -- and Haso said that it's the best with us. Haso is talking about the reserve force, they want weapons, Stole said that it was militarisation. Item 2: Transformation of the MUP - the forming of the CJB. Stole is talking about transformation of the MUP - I am not in favour. I'm actually referring to him. He was not in favour. Haso and Fikret did not want to take the badges. And then down there: I spoke about a specific agreement that would bring unison among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, could you please read the previous sentence because you didn't read it in its entirety. Not what you said but the comment about the transformation of the MUP and onwards?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The transformation of the MUP - the setting up of the CJB [as interpreted], Stole is talking about the transformation of the MUP - I'm not in favour of the splitting up of the service. Yeah, I omitted that, I'm sorry. Yeah, you're right. If you allow me to say just one more sentence about this and then we'll not go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read carefully this issue about the transformation of MUP and where it says something about the forming. What is this abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The forming of the CSB, Security Services Centre. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Say whatever you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I need to say two things. I finished with this note, but I omitted to say that as far as the badges were concerned, the tendency in the conversation between Fikret and Hasan was such that not that they didn't want to have any badges but that they were opposed to the idea to have Prijedor station detached from Banja Luka. They preferred it to be independent. I was much too brief, and -- I'm afraid -- all right. I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please, just speak slowly if possible.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to say it slowly. I'm kindly asking everybody who is listening to me and looking at this piece of paper of mine. First of all, linguistically it is totally wrong. Such sentences not exist in our language. They're totally erroneous. But the reason for that was not that I was not good in writing, but, rather, because I acquired a habit over the time of making such cryptic notes that would be clear only to me and nobody else. For that reason, it makes no sense to seek something and to read into this document. I'm the only one who can make any use of this document. And as for what I said verbally is something that you should use. This is just a kind of aid that helped me expand. For example, if you look at this doodling what I made while I was waiting, it means nothing. It would be irresponsible if I produced this as a kind of document. That was for my personal use, and that's why you have all these drawings. This was just in aid of myself and this is not an official document. This is all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jankovic. Can we go on, please. Can you tell me what was the relationship between your SJB chief, Talundzic, and Fikret Kadiric with respect to Mr. Zupljanin and the visits of the former chief. Was that the usual relationship that it is in normal times or was it a different one?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm glad that you asked me that, because in my view that is the crucial thing. While I was in the service, in many situations, the chief of the centre, which is the capacity in which Mr. Zupljanin used to visit us, was a post that was occupied by a very high ranking official, and whenever such an official comes to visit a station, including ours, we stood to attention. And everything else is done at the same level. Now, suddenly, things are taking a reverse course in this meeting. Okay, Fikret was a commander, he had vast experience in police, but Hasan had no experience whatsoever in police. Nevertheless, they were acting in such an arrogant and brazen way. They were treating us like naughty children, trying to tell us, Don't go fighting each other. You should behave yourselves. Instead, they were putting certain conditions. And this is something that was not so visible and so obvious but that was something that caused us concern.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you please repeat this portion when you said about how mother treats her children.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: So, under the current situation, the conduct turned into something opposite. The chief was acting in a very calm and polite way, trying to appease them just like a mother tries to appease children when they are being naughty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which chief are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Chief Zupljanin, the chief of the centre. All the others were just quiet, keeping quiet, acting in a neutral way. Mr. Hasan Talundzic, the chief of the station, and Mr. Kadiric were sort of putting forth certain conditions, saying, We don't want this, or we want this, et cetera. I couldn't see where this was leading to, but I did know that that was not the way to do the business in the service in -- in such a manner and that it was going to be wrong, and that's why I found it difficult to accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, apart from the persons that you mentioned and the journalists who arrived later, was anyone else present at the meeting at the Prijedor SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. All those who were present are noted down in my book. In other words, only those whose names I jotted down were present there with the exception of the two journalists who came later. As for Didovic, he did come in occasionally, but I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, after this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat what you said about Didovic because it was misrecorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Only this portion. The secretary of the chief, Mira --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Only this sentence where you mentioned Didovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat? Your microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Only the last sentence when you mentioned Didovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Didovic didn't come in. I didn't see him, but Chief Talundzic went outside, and I think that they talked there close to the door. But what they talked about, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, after this meeting, did any changes occur in the public security station with regard to the insignia and other things. I'm talking about the period leading towards the end of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: End of April 1992, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were the Serbian insignia put on, were any changes effected?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the Serbian insignia were not attached. That's for sure. I cannot remember any details. But so far as I know, we received a dispatch from the centre for everyone to wear the Serbian insignia except for Prijedor and Kotor. I can't say exactly whether I saw it myself, whether I had this dispatch in my hands or not, or somebody else told me. All I know is that we did not wear those insignia for a short period of time. In the meantime, tensions were heightening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you say Kotor, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Kotor Varos municipality. Because they had the same problems. So these two municipalities were exempt from this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on. You started talking about the heightening of tensions.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you turn the volume down. I have such a terrible noise in my earphones. As though fighter jets are flying through my head. The noise is terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Now it's fine. Thank you. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you go on? You started talking about the heightening of tensions. Continue, please. What you wanted to say. Did the situation become calm in Prijedor or were the tensions on the rise?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, tensions were on the rise every day. Now, everything was the same; only it was more of it. Now I don't have any sound in my headphones at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I get interruptions. So tensions were going up in the same style, so to speak. Now, now it's okay. There were very many minute details that I don't want to go into. All I can tell you is that one can grasp the overall situation through a mosaic of small details, but when you see certain things on a daily basis and these things are going up and up in every sense, then you realise that the tensions were heightening. Although this might sound personal and this is something that I never said to anyone, I will tell you, I omitted some of the things that were of a personal nature. For example, Chief Zupljanin said at that meeting, You, meaning we who were present there, Must agree amongst yourselves about how to resolve this. You cannot wait for someone coming from the outside to do that for you. And then Fikret said, Sir, we cannot do that because some people here are just spying upon other people. That's the word he used. And he pointed the finger at me. And then the next day he called me to his office, and I said that Ago and he were sharing an office. So Fikret called me and told me literally this. He says, You are crazy. Don't you know that it's just a matter of days when war will break out. Are you going to assume the responsibility that if you win you will not kill my family? And I will assume the responsibility that if we win I will not kill your family. I can tell you, I was never in a position of power, and I cannot make such promises to anyone. I told him, I wouldn't kill your family because that would not depend on me at all. And to tell you the truth, I'm not trusting you at all. Even if you made this promise to me, I wouldn't believe you. This was a totally unnatural conversation at the time. However, it was maybe a normal conversation given the situation that was developing. So I hope I was able to bring this reality closer to you, and that's what I meant when I said "tensions."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this period of time, was there a larger presence of armed individuals and army members in Prijedor and around it, and were there motorcades of military vehicles to be seen and did that have an impact on the general situation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me tell you that I'm not of the sort of people who frequents cafes and drinks. But there are a great many of those who do. And then you would have one cafe where members of one ethnicity would gather and the other gather in others, and there there would be talk of groups forming, weapons being procured. Of course, this was not in terms of a report that I received, something specific. Simply, you had this feeling of anticipation, waiting for that spark to hit off and lead to something major. Since there had been fighting going on in Slavonia and there were people coming back from the front line there, you were able to see out in the street people in a large variety of uniform, camouflage, olive-green, dressed partly in uniform, partly in civilian clothes, and that's how the situation was in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, could we just ask the witness what Mr. Zupljanin actually did to help resolve the problems in Prijedor? You told us that at the meeting he had asked the persons present to see if they could solve the problems by themselves. And you also told us that he exempted Prijedor and Kotor Varos from having to wear the Serbian insignia, at least for a short period of time. But what else did Mr. Zupljanin actually do to help avoid major conflicts in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, I don't know that. But I don't think that it would be the case that he would come to our office and see us only. I don't know what he did on higher levels, and I cannot talk about it. But as for the segment where I was present and when I was listening him, there wasn't a sentence that he uttered that was not aimed at easing tensions. It was a reconciliatory tone seeking to calm the situation down. He was the supervisor of us all. This is what I saw and what I can tell you about. As was the case with every member of the service and every citizen who was interested in these matters, what I heard was that he went to the municipal building to ease tensions and wasn't able to. To what extent was he successful with us? Well, let me give you an assessment of it, though I'm not best placed to do so. What was the extent of these tensions and the conflicts? Well, it was the intensity of a major fire which he tried to put out and was unable to, but he tried to a certain extent and was able to put out the fire to a certain degree. Let's say that there were a dozen of us there and if two were on one side, other two on the other side and the rest were neutral, then, of course, they were open to influence and they were open also to what he himself could tell them to tilt them either to one side or to the other. What I saw was that it was possible to reach agreement and there was need for one, and I was also able to see that those who were higher up, my superiors, and who were the ones that were the architects of my fate -- well, I'm not speaking about ministers. I did not see them that high up. But I did see that they had the opportunity to decide that fate of ours. And in that context I was a bit concerned by the fact that these two took up such a hard-line where they wouldn't desist an inch. I hope I was able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you mentioned something that isn't in the transcript. You said your higher ups did not want a war.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was something that I was interested in. Was my minister, my president of the country, or my prime minister, eager to wage a war. Well, if that is the case, then this is something that would be conveyed down to us through my superior. But that wasn't the case. This wasn't what I saw. What I saw down my hierarchy was an intention to find an agreement and I felt that this was, indeed, going to be the case, that we would find a solution and not wage a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What period of time was this between the period when Mr. Zupljanin took up his position up until April? Can you tell us, was there at some point an incidence where there was public unrest, where public law and order were disrupted? Was there some sort of an incident of any sort?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor or in the area in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the area in general.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I can't remember at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will now change topics. We will be discussing a different meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's a new topic that I would like to embark on, but I can tell that the witness is growing tired and is not as focussed on my questions as before. Perhaps we should adjourn today, since I am about to work on a topic which is quite an extensive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should rise earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We have been alerted to the difficulties that the witness was likely to have. Yes. Mr. Jankovic, we're about to take the adjournment for today. As Judge Harhoff indicated to you when you came in this morning, your testimony is likely to occupy us over several days so that the -- I would ask you to bear in mind the warning that I'm about to give you at each day's rising, and it is this. That, having been sworn as a witness and your testimony having commenced, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side in this matter, and, indeed, in such conversations as you may have with anybody outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. Do you understand what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will rise and resume your testimony tomorrow morning in this courtroom at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
